title: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit
hook: fourteen weeks, seven Upanishads, one sit to hold them all, and the three words that tie them together
tomorrow: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, the Shvetashvatara's last word. The teaching shines for one with the highest devotion. Today, the last day of the Upanishads.

Ninety-seven days ago you started with one syllable, om, chanted at a Vedic sacrifice. Since then: dogs chanting for breakfast, a boy telling the truth at a teacher's door, a woman who asked what water is woven on, a man whose head fell off for asking too much, two birds on a tree, a wheel, a swan, a pair of fire sticks. Seven books. Fourteen weeks. Today, before moving on, all seven in one sit, and the line that runs through every one.

The Chandogya came first. Uddalaka hands his son salt dissolved in water: taste it here, here, everywhere. That essence is the self of all. Tat tvam asi: you are that. The Brihadaranyaka. Yajnavalkya won't let anyone pin the self down: not this, not this. And Maitreyi asks the question that matters: what would I do with wealth that can't make me immortal? The Taittiriya: five sheaths, from food to breath to mind to understanding, and at the very center, bliss. The Aitareya: the self enters the body through the crown of the head, and near the end comes a great saying, consciousness is Brahman. The Prashna: six students wait a year to ask their questions, and every answer comes back to breath and om. The Mundaka: two kinds of knowledge, a bow and an arrow, two birds, and rivers losing their names in the sea. The Shvetashvatara: the wheel, the swan, the one Lord, and the highest devotion. Seven voices, centuries apart, read differently by different schools. Advaita teachers hear in them one reality without a second. Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers hear a self that belongs to God and is never simply erased. All of them treasure the same verses. And the thread they pull on is Uddalaka's: what you're looking for is not far away. Tat tvam asi.
screen: `CHANDOGYA: SALT IN THE WATER.` · `BRIHADARANYAKA: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `TAITTIRIYA, AITAREYA, PRASHNA.` · `MUNDAKA AND SHVETASHVATARA.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Sit in the posture from four days ago and take seven breaths, one for each book: salt everywhere; not this, not this; inward, sheath by sheath, to joy; consciousness is Brahman; the breath itself; the river reaching the sea; devotion, in whatever form is yours. Then let the rest of the sit be quiet, with three words underneath it: you are that.

Uddalaka, the sage who taught his son with salt dissolved in water. Ninety-eight sessions in seven of the principal Upanishads, from om at the Chandogya's opening to bhakti in the Shvetashvatara's last verse, carry his thread.
Your line: tat tvam asi, you are that. Tomorrow, a new text begins, the Yoga Sutras. Block A, done.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions treat these Upanishads as the heart of the Vedanta: students chant and study them with a teacher, and the great sayings, such as tat tvam asi and prajnanam brahma, are taught as summaries of the whole.

fork.setup: after seven Upanishads, a friend asks you for the one line that ties them together. which line does this session pick?
options: tat tvam asi: you are that.
fork.reveal: all three are real lines from the block. the session picks Uddalaka's tat tvam asi as the thread: what you seek is not far away.

original.note: Sanskrit tat tvam asi: that you are. Chandogya 6.8.7 and the verses after it.

trapdoor: what you thought: tat tvam asi is a slogan.
what it means: the essence of everything and your own deepest self are not two separate things far apart.

what a scholar hears: one of four mahavakyas, great sayings, traditionally one from each Veda; Advaita reads it as identity, Vishishtadvaita as inseparable relation, and Madhva's Dvaita reads the phrase differently again.

chat.meaning: The thread through all seven is Uddalaka's: tat tvam asi, you are that. What you're looking for is not far away.

Uddalaka.meaning: the sage who taught his son with salt in water

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who said of the self: not this, not this

notes: Block A close (days 332–429): names all seven Upanishads and points to Block B, the Yoga Sutras.
Aitareya: prajnanam brahma comes near the end (3.3); confirm placement.
Dvaita (Madhva) reading of tat tvam asi: Madhva's school reads the sandhi as 'sa atma atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), or as likeness; described only as 'reads the phrase differently'.
Mahavakyas, one from each Veda: prajnanam brahma (Rig, Aitareya), aham brahmasmi (Yajur, Brihadaranyaka), tat tvam asi (Sama, Chandogya), ayam atma brahma (Atharva, Mandukya).

Audit (10% sample): factual fixes. The Chandogya was called 'first and longest', but the Brihadaranyaka is the longest (day 360 says so); 'the seven principal Upanishads' corrected to 'seven of the principal Upanishads' (the usual list of principal Upanishads is ten or more, including Isha, Kena, Katha and Mandukya, not read in this block); 'ninety-eight sessions ago' corrected to ninety-seven days ago.
